citation: Bucol, A. A., Dangan-Galon, F., & Alcala, A. C. (2017). Catch-per-unit effort of exploited finfishes and crustaceans in Ilog River Estuary, Negros Occidental, Philippines. PeerJ Preprints, 5:e2957v1. https://doi.org/10.7287/peerj.preprints.2957v1; Bucol, A. A., Aspilla, P. S., Dangan-Galon, F., Tababa, R. T., & Pacalioga, J. O. (2018). The 2013 fish kill event in Ilog River-Estuary, Negros Occidental, Philippines. The Philippine Scientist, 53–55, 52–65; Oñate-Pacalioga, J., & Peralta, A. (2016). Fish species abundance and species richness in a diverted channel in Ilog, Negros Occidental, Philippines. Manila Journal of Science, 9, 91–104.

peerjPreprint.publicationStatus: Version 1 preprint posted 2 May 2017; a peer-reviewed journal version was not verified in this review.
peerjPreprint.license: The preprint copy identifies CC BY 4.0. This applies to the identified preprint version; it is not a blanket license for other related articles, maps, or external material.
peerjPreprint.scope: Reports catch-per-unit-effort monitoring of finfish and crustacean fisheries at the Malabong outlet/main Ilog River Estuary, not the whole Ilog-Hilabangan catchment.
peerjPreprint.sampling: The paper reports trawl and beach-seine sampling in April, May, September, October, and December 2013 and January 2014. Its abstract describes catch monitoring that also includes mud-crab pots; gear coverage and dates should remain tied to the methods in the preprint.
peerjPreprint.richnessStatement: The Results state that 85 fish species from 49 families and nine orders were known in Ilog River Estuary, then say species-diversity and taxonomic details would appear in a separate paper in preparation. No complete fish checklist or species-by-station table was located in this source.
peerjPreprint.eventDateCaveat: The preprint refers to a fish-kill event on 19 April 2013, while the later Philippine Scientist article reports 22–26 April 2013. Do not collapse these into one confirmed date without checking the underlying records.

fishKillArticle.publicationStatus: The article is identified as The Philippine Scientist, volume 53–55 (2018), pages 52–65; the author-shared full text is available through ResearchGate.
fishKillArticle.publisherAndRights: The article page reproduces a 2018 University of San Carlos Press copyright notice. USC Publishing House policy says accepted authors sign a copyright-transfer agreement before publication. No article-specific open license or permission for a structured derivative was verified.
fishKillArticle.evidenceScope: The paper documents a historical fish-kill event and water-quality observations in the Malabong Ilog River-Estuary; it is an environmental-event study, not a fish-community checklist, current water-quality reading, or present-day safety assessment.

divertedChannelStudy.discoveryEvidence: The 2018 Ilog fish-kill paper cites Oñate-Pacalioga and Peralta (2016), Fish species abundance and species richness in a diverted channel in Ilog, Negros Occidental, Philippines, Manila Journal of Science 9:91–104, and attributes a local waste/sewage finding to that study. The DLSU repository issue archive was searched, but an article-specific record or complete primary text was not retrieved.
divertedChannelStudy.reuse: Article-specific terms could not be checked because the primary item was not retrieved. No table, species list, or derivative data were transcribed.

decision.use: Keep the PeerJ preprint as a dated estuarine fisheries-method and source-discovery lead. Retain the fish-kill article as historical environmental-event evidence. Treat the diverted-channel article as an unverified bibliographic lead pending primary retrieval.
decision.regionalCompletionCount: Do not use the preprint's 85-species statement as a complete checklist, verified regional denominator, current-presence total, or completeness score.
decision.currentSafetyAlert: none; the reported event is historical and does not describe present conditions
decision.reason: The preprint is explicitly a CPUE report and defers species diversity and taxonomy details to another paper. The later journal article covers a dated environmental event rather than a checklist, and the cited 2016 diverted-channel primary text remains inaccessible in this review.

limitations: The Malabong outlet site is one estuarine part of the larger Ilog-Hilabangan system; these observations do not cover all river reaches or tributaries.

The 85-species richness statement is attributed to a 2017 preprint whose Results defer the species and taxonomic details to a separate paper in preparation; it is not a checklist in the reviewed source.
The PeerJ item is version 1 preprint evidence, not a verified peer-reviewed final version.
The preprint's fish-kill date and the later journal article's event-date range differ; preserve both source statements until reconciled.
The 2018 fish-kill paper is historical evidence only and cannot support a current safety alert or present water-quality status.
The 2016 diverted-channel paper is known only through a citation in the 2018 article; its sampling scope, taxa, methods, coordinate detail, and reuse terms remain unverified.
No current occupancy, catchability, legal fishing advice, diet, present abundance, river boundary, or regional species completeness is established.
No species table, map, coordinate, occurrence assertion, diet record, current safety alert, or public app row was added.
nextActions: Seek the separate Ilog ichthyofauna/taxonomy paper mentioned as in preparation in the 2017 preprint, or ask the study authors or Silliman University-Angelo King Center for Research and Environmental Management whether a completed checklist, station matrix, vouchers, and dates are available.
Retrieve and review the cited 2016 diverted-channel paper from the DLSU Manila Journal of Science archive or authors before using any of its species, abundance, or water-quality results.

If preparing a public derivative from the PeerJ version 1 preprint, retain its exact citation and CC BY 4.0 attribution and keep each source-version claim traceable; do not combine its estuarine richness statement with freshwater-only checklists.
Continue the Visayas freshwater source sweep with Siaton and other Negros waterbodies; do not convert historical fish-kill evidence into a live alert.
